strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated core idea: exploiting the additive/combinatorial structure of combinatorial synthesis libraries so that predictions for all 10^10+ products can be computed from only O(|S|) cached synthon associative contributions, enabling approximate-but-exhaustive top-k retrieval in seconds on a single consumer GPU. The runtime analysis (Section 3.3) and GPU top-k implementation details (Appendix A.3) are concrete and credible.

Significant reproducibility contribution: the authors construct and release an open 10B-compound CSL derived from ZINC22/BRICS, with 12M compounds exhaustively annotated with docking scores on five diverse targets and physicochemical properties, plus code and trained weights. This is a genuinely useful benchmark for the virtual screening community.

Evaluation covers multiple angles: Recall-j-at-k against exhaustive ground truth (Figure 3), constraint satisfaction across four standard drug-likeness rule sets, a matched-budget comparison against Thompson sampling (Figure 8), and end-to-end runtime measurements on 12M and 10B libraries (Table 1).

Data-leakage handling is described explicitly (surrogate trained only on the 1M library; evaluation on 12M/10B), and the paper is generally honest about design choices (e.g., no extensive hyperparameter tuning, synthetic feasibility not ensured).
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the hierarchical synthon/R-group/reaction encoders and library representation are taken from Pedawi et al. (2022). The new elements are the additive factorization into synthon associative contributions and the noise-injection trick; the latter's claimed robustness to errors-in-variables (Griliches, 1974) is asserted with a citation but never demonstrated theoretically or empirically (no ablation with/without noise).

Surrogate quality is modest and weakly analyzed: Figure 7 shows docking-score R-squared of roughly 0.3-0.55, and the factorized surrogate degrades noticeably for several endpoints. The paper does not disentangle how much of the retrieval error comes from the surrogate versus the factorization step, nor does it analyze when the additive approximation fails (e.g., properties with strong synthon-interaction effects).

Retrieval accuracy is not uniformly strong: recall of the true top-100 at k=100,000 varies substantially across targets and constraint sets (roughly 0.1-0.8 in Figure 3), and the manuscript does not discuss what these numbers imply about how many high-scoring compounds remain missed in practice.

Baseline comparison is thin: the only non-trivial baseline is Thompson sampling, restricted to the unconstrained setting on the top five reactions of the 12M library. No comparison with V-SYNTHES, NGT, or other established screening methods, and no comparison against a simple brute-force surrogate-encoder evaluation on the 12M library to quantify the factorization's cost/accuracy trade-off.

The 10B-library results (Figure 4) are circular: with no ground truth scores at that scale, enrichment is measured against surrogate predictions that APEX itself optimizes, so this experiment demonstrates scale/runtime more than retrieval quality.

No limitations section; the paper does not discuss generalization to real commercial libraries like Enamine REAL (whose reactions and synthons differ substantially from BRICS-derived ones), the accuracy caveats of the fast GPU Vina implementation, or the implications of ignoring synthetic feasibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important problem: exhaustive evaluation of ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries is computationally prohibitive, and the proposed factorized surrogate enables screening of a 10B-compound library in seconds on a single consumer GPU, which is a compelling engineering result.

The construction of an open benchmark CSL (10B compounds, with a fully enumerated 12M subset exhaustively annotated with docking scores on five diverse targets and RDKit physicochemical properties) is a valuable community contribution that enables ground-truth top-k evaluation, which prior proprietary libraries (e.g., Enamine REAL) do not permit.

The methodology is clearly formalized (Sections 3.1–3.4), the factorization from surrogate embeddings to synthon-level additive contributions is cleanly derived, and the GPU implementation details (chain-of-batches with CCCL AIR top-k) are documented in the appendix.

The recall-j-at-k metric computed against an exhaustively scored ground truth is the right evaluation, and the authors are upfront that APEX provides 'exact retrieval of approximate top-k sets' rather than exact top-k of the true objective.
Code, datasets, and trained model weights are stated to be released, supporting reproducibility of the pipeline and benchmark.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The hierarchical library representation (synthon/R-group/reaction encoders) and the factorizer design are taken directly from Pedawi et al. (2022), which the authors acknowledge. The genuinely new elements are (a) observing that a linear prediction head over a factorized additive embedding yields additive per-synthon property contributions, and (b) a GPU top-k implementation reusing the existing AIR algorithm (Zhang et al., 2023). This is primarily an applications/engineering contribution that is thin for the ICML main track.

The surrogate quality is weak where it matters most. Figure 7 shows R-squared of roughly 0.3–0.5 for the docking score endpoints (e.g., score_ESR1 and score_F10 well below 0.4), and the factorized surrogate is consistently worse than the original surrogate. Consequently, Figure 3A shows that with k = 100,000 (0.8% of the 12M library), recall of the true top-100 is frequently below 0.5 for several target/constraint combinations—i.e., most of the true top compounds are missed. The claim of 'consistently strong performance' in the abstract overstates these results.

The errors-in-variables argument (Eq. 4, Griliches 1974) for robustness of the factorized predictions is asserted but not substantiated. There is no theoretical result or empirical verification that the factorizer's reconstruction error distribution matches the isotropic training noise p(ε), so the claimed mitigation of errors-in-variables is essentially hand-wavy.

The comparison with Thompson sampling is not cost-matched. The APEX surrogate is trained on an exhaustively docked 1M-compound library (millions of expensive docking evaluations that TS never consumes), yet the budget comparison counts only TS's |S|·w + i evaluations. Counting the surrogate's label acquisition cost would likely reverse the conclusion at low budgets. Moreover, the TS comparison is restricted to the top five reactions and the unconstrained setting only.

Missing comparison to the most relevant baseline: V-SYNTHES (Sadybekov et al., 2022), a hierarchical synthon-based screening method the authors themselves cite, is not evaluated. Comparing only against Thompson sampling and a random baseline is insufficient to establish the claimed superiority over existing virtual screening approaches.

All quantitative recall evaluation is performed on the single self-constructed 12M library; the 10B results are limited to runtime and score-distribution enrichment (Figure 4) without any retrieval-accuracy validation, because the 10B library is never exhaustively scored. The generalization gap between 1M-trained surrogate and 10B-library evaluation, including out-of-distribution synthon combinations, is not analyzed.

The benchmark CSL is built by BRICS recombination of ZINC22 molecules with no guarantee of synthetic feasibility ('we do not consider or ensure synthetic feasibility'), which weakens the relevance of the drug-discovery claims relative to real make-on-demand libraries like Enamine REAL.

The paper contains no limitations section. Key limitations—surrogate error propagation to retrieval quality, the large upfront labeling cost, applicability only to additive-factorizable structure, and the synthetic-feasibility gap—are never honestly discussed, and several abstract-level claims are stronger than the evidence supports.
Presentation issues: Figure 2 is cluttered and largely illegible, Figure 3 panels are small with hard-to-read legends, and the footnote with the code URL appears broken/empty in the manuscript.

strengths: The core technical idea is clean and well-executed: factorizing surrogate property predictions into additive synthon-level 'associative contributions' makes exhaustive evaluation of a 10B-compound library tractable on a single consumer GPU, a genuinely useful capability for virtual screening.

The design choices are technically sound and well-motivated: noise injection during surrogate training (Eq. 4) to mitigate the errors-in-variables problem induced by the factorized approximation, a lexicographic priority-queue scheme (Eq. 18) for handling constraints, and a well-documented GPU implementation (chain-of-batches with CCCL AIR top-k) with strong reported runtimes (top-1M from 10B compounds in ~30s on a T4).

A significant community contribution: the authors release an open, fully enumerated benchmark CSL (12M compounds exhaustively docked against five diverse targets plus physicochemical properties, backed by a 10B virtual library), addressing the lack of reproducible alternatives to proprietary libraries like Enamine REAL.

Careful experimental hygiene: the surrogate is trained only on the 1M library, runtime is measured end-to-end, TS baselines use matched evaluation budgets, and code, data, and model weights are released.
The paper is clearly written, with the method formalized precisely (Eqs. 1-18) and the amortization/compute arguments made concrete (memory and FLOP analysis in Section 3.3).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the hierarchical synthon/R-group/reaction representation and factorizer design is directly adapted from Pedawi et al. (2022); the main contribution is repurposing that architecture as an additive score approximation for exhaustive top-k retrieval rather than a new modeling principle.

Baseline comparison is thin. The only algorithmic baseline is Thompson sampling, and only in the unconstrained setting (because the TS implementation does not support constraints). No comparison against hierarchical screening methods such as V-SYNTHES, active-learning-based approaches, or simpler alternatives (e.g., synthon-level filtering or beam search over the CSL), making it hard to assess how much of the gain comes from the factorization versus merely evaluating a surrogate exhaustively.

Surrogate quality is modest: Figure 7 shows R-squared around 0.4-0.6 for the docking endpoints, and factorization further degrades some endpoints. This raises questions about how faithful the 'approximate-but-exhaustive' top-k sets are, particularly since retrieval accuracy is only quantified on the 12M library and not validated against exhaustively scored subsets at larger scale.

Retrieval performance, while far above random, is not uniformly strong: recall of the true top-100 at k=100,000 is often only ~0.3-0.5 for the more stringent constraint sets (Figure 3A), and the paper does not analyze failure modes or when the additive factorization breaks down.

Potential subtle leakage/in-sample concern: the factorizer is trained on the 12M library that is also used for the ground-truth top-k evaluation (albeit without labels), and the evaluation library overlaps structurally with the 1M training library by construction (downsampled reactions).

No limitations section or discussion of scope: the method assumes objective/constraint properties are well-approximated by additive synthon contributions; objectives like co-folding or non-additive ADMET endpoints may violate this, and generalization to genuinely novel synthons is not examined.

The 'ground truth' is Vina docking scores, which are themselves a noisy proxy for binding; the practical significance of high recall against Vina top-k is asserted rather than demonstrated with any downstream validation (e.g., hit triage or experimental evidence).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: factorizing surrogate predictions into per-synthon associative contributions reduces exhaustive scoring over a 10B-compound library to cached lookups over ~10^5 synthon vectors, a genuinely new application of factorization-based retrieval to virtual screening of CSLs.

Substantial practical impact demonstrated empirically: end-to-end retrieval of top-k=1M from a 10B library in ~21s on a single T4 GPU, with an order-of-magnitude GPU-vs-CPU speedup and scaling to the 70B Enamine REAL library zero-shot.

Valuable community resource: an open 10B-compound BRICS CSL plus fully enumerated 12M and 1M subsets annotated with ground-truth Vina docking scores on five diverse targets and 23 RDKit physicochemical properties, enabling ground-truth top-k evaluation of any screening method. Code, data, and model weights are released, supporting reproducibility.

Honest and reasonably thorough evaluation: recall is reported against exact ground-truth top-j sets across multiple constraint sets (Figure 2), compared to the relevant synthon-space Thompson sampling baseline under matched budgets, and the surrogate-vs-factorizer error decomposition (Appendix A.6) cleanly separates error sources and shows the cross-term is negligible.
The zero-shot transfer experiment to Enamine REAL is a meaningful test of generality, and the authors candidly note its limits (e.g., degraded enrichment for MET, likely fixable by fine-tuning).
weaknesses: Retrieval accuracy is moderate rather than compelling in absolute terms: at k=100,000 (0.8% of the 12M library), recall of the ground-truth top-100 is roughly 0.3-0.8 depending on target and constraint set, and recall of top-j for j>=1000 is often below 0.2 at that budget. This is honestly reported, but it means APEX misses a substantial fraction of true top compounds, which tempers the practical value of the 'approximate-but-exhaustive' claim.

The benchmark CSL is synthetic and idealized: it is constructed via BRICS fragmentation of ZINC22 molecules without any guarantee of synthetic feasibility, and reactions are combinatorial recombinations rather than curated medicinal-chemistry reactions. Real CSLs (e.g., Enamine REAL) have different synthon/reaction statistics, so the demonstrated recall and factorization quality may not transfer; the 12M/10B library also shares its synthon/reaction family with the training data, limiting assessment of distribution shift (the Enamine experiment partially addresses this but lacks ground-truth labels).

The errors-in-variables argument for why noise-augmented training makes the factorized prediction robust (Section 4.3) is heuristic; no theoretical guarantee is given on how the additive factorization error scales with synthon interaction strength, and the paper does not analyze which endpoint/chemistry regimes break the additivity assumption.

Baseline comparison is thin: only Thompson sampling is compared, and only on the five largest reactions in the unconstrained setting. Stronger baselines such as V-SYNTHES, active learning/surrogate iterative filtering (Deep Docking, MolPal), or library-constrained generative methods (CSLVAE/NGT) are discussed but not empirically compared.

The oracle itself is approximate (Vina docking scores), so 'ground truth top-k' reflects a noisy objective; the paper does not discuss how surrogate and factorization error interact with oracle noise, which matters for claims about downstream hit-finding utility.

Training details are intentionally minimal (d=64, 'no extensive hyperparameter tuning'), which supports the lightweight claim but leaves open how much accuracy scales with model capacity or better factorizer architectures; the ablation space is unexplored.

strengths: The core idea of factorizing surrogate predictions into cached per-synthon associative contributions is elegant and yields a genuinely large runtime gain, enabling exhaustive top-k search over 10B+ compound libraries on a single consumer GPU (Table 1 shows ~21s for k=1M on a 10B library vs. ~148s on CPU, and >3 minutes for the 70B Enamine library).

The paper contributes a useful, fully annotated open benchmark: a 10B compound BRICS-based CSL with 12M and 1M fully enumerated subsets, exhaustively docked against five diverse targets (PARP1, MET, DRD2, F10, ESR1) plus 28 physicochemical endpoints, enabling exact ground-truth top-k evaluation for any objective/constraint query. Code, data, and model weights are promised, which supports reproducibility.

The evaluation protocol is sensible: surrogate trained only on the 1M library with evaluation on 12M/10B libraries to avoid leakage; Figure 10 usefully isolates the cost of the factorization step by comparing recall of the surrogate vs. factorized surrogate; Appendix A.6 provides a clean error decomposition (surrogate vs. factorizer error) that is practically informative.

The methodological framing (declarative queries, amortization across changing constraints/objectives, one-time training vs. per-campaign retraining) addresses a real workflow pain point in ultra-large library screening that iterative methods like active learning or generative approaches do not handle well.
Appendix material (CSL formalism, GPU top-k implementation details, constraint sets, architecture details) is thorough and mostly self-contained.
weaknesses: Absolute retrieval accuracy is moderate at best, yet the paper's framing ('exact retrieval of approximate top-k sets', 'consistently strong performance') risks overstating it. At a budget of k=100,000 (0.8% of the 12M library), recall of the ground-truth top-100 is only ~0.55-0.77 unconstrained (Figure 2A), and drops further under constraints and for larger j. Random is 0.008, so there is clear signal, but 25-45% of the true top compounds are missed in the best case; the practical consequence of these misses is not discussed.

The additive synthon factorization (Eq. 12/17) fundamentally assumes molecular properties decompose as sums of per-synthon contributions, ignoring synthon-synthon interaction effects. For non-additive endpoints like docking scores this is a strong approximation. The paper reports factorized vs. surrogate R-squared dropping for several endpoints (Figure 6A: e.g., MET, F10 around 0.25-0.45), but the implications for top-k fidelity are not rigorously connected to the recall results, and the errors-in-variables justification for noise injection (Eq. 5) is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The benchmark CSL has questionable chemical validity: it is built by BRICS recombination of ZINC22 fragments with no synthetic feasibility check, explicitly acknowledged by the authors ('we do not consider or ensure synthetic feasibility'). The ground-truth oracle is itself a 2D docking score (AutoDock Vina), which is a crude proxy for binding affinity. This limits the evidential value of the retrieval experiments for actual drug discovery use.

Baseline comparisons are thin. The only quantitative baseline is Thompson sampling (Klarich et al., 2024), restricted to the five largest reactions of the 12M library and unable to handle constraints. V-SYNTHES (Sadybekov et al., 2022), the most prominent synthon-based hierarchical screening method, is discussed but not compared; neither are active learning baselines (e.g., MolPal-style surrogate + acquisition) on the 12M library, where matched-budget comparison would be feasible. The claim of superiority over 'alternative methods' thus rests on one comparison against one method.

The 10B and 70B library experiments (Figures 7) provide no ground-truth verification: enrichment is shown only against background distributions and against top-k sets of the smaller library, and the zero-shot Enamine transfer is validated only via R-squared on random samples (Figure 6). Distribution shift for extreme extrapolation from a 1M training set to a 70B foreign library is not assessed on the actual retrieval task.

The architecture is notably lightweight (d=64, ~160K-680K parameters, 'no extensive hyperparameter tuning'), which is fine as a demonstration, but it makes it hard to judge whether the observed factorizer error is intrinsic to the additive factorization or an artifact of an undersized model; no scaling analysis of model capacity vs. factorization accuracy is provided.

Some presentation issues: the runtime analysis in Section 4.3 (3 TFLOP claim) ignores top-k maintenance overhead until later, the emphasis on 'exact retrieval' can mislead readers into over-interpreting retrieval fidelity, and key recall figures would benefit from per-target statistical treatment rather than aggregate curves with standard deviations only in the appendix.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: virtual screening over ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs) is a real bottleneck in drug discovery, and the 'approximate-but-exhaustive' framing—exhaustive evaluation of an approximate surrogate rather than partial evaluation of an expensive oracle—is a clean and useful conceptual contribution.

The core technical idea is sound and elegant: factorizing surrogate predictions into cached per-synthon associative contributions reduces exhaustive scoring of a 10B-compound library to a few TFLOPs, enabling top-k retrieval over tens of billions of compounds in seconds on a single T4 GPU. The errors-in-variables motivation for training the surrogate with embedding noise (Sec. 4.3) is a thoughtful statistical argument connecting surrogate training to factorization robustness.

Significant community contribution in the form of an open, fully annotated benchmark: a 10B-compound BRICS-based CSL with a 12M exhaustively docked subset (5 targets via AutoDock Vina) plus 28 RDKit physicochemical endpoints, enabling exact ground-truth top-k evaluation for arbitrary objective/constraint queries. This addresses a genuine reproducibility gap relative to proprietary libraries like Enamine REAL.

Evaluation is multi-faceted: top-j-at-k recall under six constraint sets, constraint satisfaction rates, recall-vs-budget curves comparing the factorized and non-factorized surrogate, a comparison against Thompson sampling (Klarich et al., 2024) at matched budgets, docking score enrichment on the 70B Enamine REAL library zero-shot, and detailed runtime benchmarks (GPU vs CPU, varying k and constraints).

The appendix provides valuable supporting analysis: an error decomposition (surrogate error vs. factorizer error, with a negligible cross term, Appendix A.6/Fig. 8), full architecture and training details, and the GPU top-k implementation description. Code and model weights are released.
The paper is honest about limitations in places, e.g., no synthetic feasibility guarantees, no extensive hyperparameter tuning, and degraded zero-shot performance on MET in the Enamine application.
weaknesses: Retrieval accuracy is more modest than the framing suggests. At k = 100,000 (0.8% of the 12M library), recall of the ground truth top-100 is roughly 0.75–0.8 unconstrained but drops substantially under tighter constraint sets (e.g., ~0.3–0.5 for Astex Rule of 3 and Pfizer 3/75), and for j = 100,000 it falls below ~0.2 (Fig. 2). The abstract's claim of 'consistently strong performance' and the conclusion's 'high recall rates' overstate what the figures show; many true top compounds remain missed.

Fig. 10 undercuts the central value proposition: at matched evaluation budgets, the non-factorized surrogate (which requires no library-structural assumption) achieves recall comparable to, and often slightly better than, the APEX-factorized surrogate. This indicates the factorization contributes speed and amortization rather than retrieval quality, and that APEX's accuracy is bounded by the surrogate's sample-based performance. The paper does not clearly acknowledge or discuss this near-parity.

The baseline comparison is narrow. Thompson sampling is the only external method, run unconstrained and only on the five largest reactions of the 12M library. No comparison to V-SYNTHES (the natural synthon-based baseline for docking), active learning (MolPal-style), or dense-retrieval methods (ConPLex/DrugCLIP), despite these being discussed at length in related work. This makes it hard to judge APEX's practical standing among screening approaches.

The additive synthon-contribution assumption is a strong modeling restriction for docking: protein-ligand interactions often involve coupled contributions across fragments (e.g., a hinge binder bridging two synthons), which a sum of per-(R-group, synthon) terms cannot represent. The paper quantifies the resulting factorizer error but does not analyze when or why the additive model fails, nor compare against interaction-aware factorizations (e.g., pairwise or bilinear synthon-synthon terms).

Data leakage and validity concerns: the surrogate is trained on a 1M-compound subset while evaluation uses the 12M/10B libraries built by the same BRICS fragmentation of ZINC22 molecules; synthon overlap between the labeled 1M and the evaluation libraries is not discussed, so generalization to 'new' chemical matter may be overstated. Additionally, the abstract promises a benchmark of 'more than 10 million compounds' while the fully enumerated labeled set is 12M—the 10B library itself has no ground-truth labels, so claims about the 10B/70B libraries rest on distributional enrichment (eCDFs) rather than retrieval accuracy.

Zero-shot transfer to Enamine REAL shows material degradation (MET's factorized R-squared drops sharply, and enrichment is weakest there), indicating the method is sensitive to library/reaction shift; the paper mentions this but does not probe causes or remedies.

Minor presentation issues: incomplete code URL in the footnote ('https://github.com/ Please refer to the README'), a typo in the abstract ('physicohemical'), Figure 1 is dense and hard to parse, and some claims (e.g., 'theoretical underpinnings') overstate what is a fairly straightforward linear-factorization argument.
